title: Uesugi Yozan Rescues a Bankrupt Domain
text:
In 1767 a teenager named Uesugi Harunori, later known as Yozan, became lord of the Yonezawa domain in northern Japan. He had been adopted into the Uesugi family from a smaller house. Yonezawa was crushed by debt, its population shrinking, and its leaders had seriously considered handing the domain back to the shogunate.

Yozan began with himself. He cut his own household spending sharply, wore cotton instead of silk, and ate plain meals. He then pushed reforms across the domain: planting mulberry for silk, lacquer trees and other crops, developing local weaving, opening new land, and reviving a domain school to train capable officials regardless of rank.

The reforms met resistance. In 1773 seven senior retainers petitioned against them. Yozan investigated, rejected the petition, and punished the leaders. Then he carried on.

When he retired in 1785 he gave his successor three principles: the domain belongs to the ancestors and descendants, not the lord; the people belong to the domain, not the lord; and the lord exists for the domain and its people. Yonezawa's finances recovered over the following decades, and Uchimura Kanzo later chose him as one of his Representative Men of Japan.
lesson: If you ask an organization to tighten its belt, start with your own. Reform is believed when the leader is the first to pay for it.
source: Yonezawa domain records; Uchimura Kanzo, Representative Men of Japan (1908)
